sections.title: The pipeline, end to end
sections.body:
RAG has two phases that run at different times. **Ingestion** runs ahead of time on your documents. **Query time** runs on every question.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: A RAG pipeline with its failure points
  accDescr: Documents are loaded, split into chunks, embedded and stored with metadata during ingestion. At question time the question is turned into a query, matching chunks are retrieved with an access filter, ranked, put into a prompt, and the model answers with citations. Numbered failure points mark where it can go wrong: loading, chunking, retrieval, ranking, generation and citation.
  subgraph ING[Ingestion, before any question]
    A[Load and clean documents] --> B[Split into chunks]
    B --> C[Embed and index with metadata]
  end
  subgraph QRY[Query time, every question]
    Q[Question] --> R[Retrieve with access filter]
    R --> K[Rank and trim]
    K --> P[Build the prompt]
    P --> G[Model answers and cites]
    G --> V[Check, then show the answer]
  end
  C -.-> R
  F1[F1 missing or garbled text] -.-> A
  F2[F2 answer split or context lost] -.-> B
  F3[F3 right chunk not retrieved] -.-> R
  F4[F4 right chunk buried or crowded out] -.-> K
  F5[F5 wrong or invented answer] -.-> G
  F6[F6 citation does not support the claim] -.-> V
```

The steps, in plain words:

1. **Load and clean:** read the files (PDF, web page, table), remove page furniture, keep the title and date.
2. **Chunk:** cut each document into pieces small enough to match a question and large enough to hold a whole fact (lesson 28).
3. **Embed and index:** turn each chunk into a vector (lesson 4) and store it with its text, source id, date and who may see it. Many systems also build a keyword index (lesson 29).
4. **Retrieve:** turn the question into a query, search, and keep only chunks the asker may see.
5. **Rank and trim:** order the candidates, optionally with a second, more careful model, and keep the best few that fit the prompt.
6. **Prompt:** place the chunks, the question and rules: answer only from the sources, cite them, say so when the sources do not contain the answer.
7. **Generate, cite, check:** the model answers; code checks what it can (the citation exists, a figure appears in the source).

Microsoft's overview lists five challenges that this pipeline must meet: understanding what the user meant, reaching content spread over many systems, staying inside token limits, responding in seconds, and security and governance. Keep them in mind as a checklist.
sections.example: Fictional, using the code in this lesson's lab. 'What does ERR-4417 mean?' enters at step 4; the retrieval step finds the chunk 'Runbook: common pipeline errors > ERR-4417 schema drift'; the answer quotes the sentence and cites runbook-errors#1.
sections.common_mistake: Believing RAG means 'give the model a database'. The model sees only the few chunks you place in its prompt; everything the pipeline did not retrieve does not exist for that answer.
sections.check_question: Which steps run before any question is asked, and which run on every question?
sections.check_answer: Ingestion (load and clean, chunk, embed and index) runs ahead of time. Retrieval, ranking, prompting, generation and checking run on every question.

sections.title: Where it fails: six failure points
sections.body:
RAG failures are not all 'hallucination'. Naming the step where a failure happens tells you what to fix. Here are the six marked in the figure, with what each looks like and one check:

| Point | What it looks like | One check |
|---|---|---|
| **F1 Loading** | The answer is 'not found' for a fact you know is in the file; a PDF table became a jumble | Search the stored chunk text for a sentence you know is there |
| **F2 Chunking** | The fact is cut in half, or a chunk has a fact but not what it is about (a number with no subject) | Read the chunks around a known fact |
| **F3 Retrieval** | The right document exists but never appears in the top results | Does the gold document appear in the top 3 or 5 for your test questions? (the **hit rate**) |
| **F4 Ranking and assembly** | The right chunk is retrieved but placed low, or crowded out by near-duplicates; a long prompt buries it (the 'lost in the middle' effect) | Compare answers when the right chunk is first and when it is in the middle |
| **F5 Generation** | The right chunk is in the prompt and the answer is still wrong, or adds a claim the source does not make | Compare the answer with the chunk, sentence by sentence (faithfulness) |
| **F6 Citation** | A source is cited, but it does not say what the answer claims | Open each cited chunk and check |

In our own demo (22 answerable questions, a keyword-and-vector hybrid, a deliberately simple answer step) the numbers show why this split matters: the cited chunk came from the right document for **19 of 22** questions, but the answer actually contained the right fact for only **15 of 22**. Counting only retrieval would have looked 4 questions better than the system really was. The gap is F4 and F5: the right chunk was retrieved and the answer step still picked the wrong sentence. Our answer step is a crude quotation picker, so 15 is not a prediction for a real model. The point is that the two measurements differ and must be reported separately.

Anthropic reports a related effect on the retrieval side: adding context to each chunk before embedding lowered their retrieval failure rate from 5.7 to 3.7 percent, adding keyword scoring took it to 2.9, and adding a reranker to 1.9 percent. Those are their datasets and their definition of failure, so treat them as a sign that retrieval design matters, not as numbers you will get.
sections.example: Fictional. A user asks 'Is the old 20-day annual leave rule still current?' and the system cites the superseded 2024 policy. Which failure point is that? Retrieval returned a stale document (F3, with a metadata fix: ingest dates and prefer the newest version). In our demo this question was one of the three retrieval failures.
sections.common_mistake: Calling every bad answer a hallucination. A wrong answer from the right chunk and a wrong answer because the right chunk was never retrieved need opposite fixes.
sections.check_question: Retrieval found the right document for 19 of 22 questions but only 15 of 22 answers were correct. Name the two kinds of failure and one fix for each.
sections.check_answer: 3 questions failed at retrieval (F3): improve chunking, hybrid search, metadata such as version dates. 4 more failed after retrieval (F4/F5): improve ranking and the prompt, use a better generator, check the answer against the chunk.

sections.title: Security trimming: filter before you rank
sections.body:
The most expensive RAG mistake is showing someone text they are not allowed to see. Microsoft's overview calls the fix **security trimming**: only content the asker is entitled to is considered, using permission metadata stored with each chunk or filters applied at query time. The rule is to filter **before** ranking, not after:

- If you retrieve the top 3 and then remove forbidden ones, a user may get nothing, or the forbidden chunk may influence ranking.
- If you tell the model in the prompt 'do not reveal salaries', you have asked it to behave. A prompt is advice. A filter in code is control (lesson 23).
- The caller's identity must come from a verified source (a signed-in session), never from the question text.

Our reference code does it in one line: `visible = lambda i: index.chunks[i]['acl'] in ('all', *groups)` and passes it into the search. In the demo, the question 'How big is the annual bonus pool for the finance team?' returns `Not in the documents.` for a caller with no groups, and the bonus sentence for a caller in the finance group. That is the test to keep: **same question, two callers, different answers, and the restricted text never appears for the wrong one.**

Be careful with a related limit on one platform. The Databricks documentation we read (page updated 2026-09-14) says AI Search (the product page now uses that name for what was Vector Search) does not support row-level or column-level permissions on an index. On such a platform you design access with separate indexes per audience, or with a metadata filter that your application enforces. That is lesson 32.
sections.example:
```text
caller groups=none      -> Not in the documents.
caller groups=finance   -> The annual bonus pool for the finance team is 8 percent of departmental budget, paid in March. [finance-bonus#0]
```
sections.common_mistake: Filtering the model's answer instead of the retrieved chunks. By then the forbidden text was already in the prompt, and in your logs.
sections.check_question: Why is 'tell the model not to reveal restricted documents' not enough?
sections.check_answer: A prompt instruction is advice the model may not follow, or an attacker may talk it out of. The restricted text should never be retrieved for that user, which only a filter applied in code before ranking guarantees.

sections.title: Not in the documents: abstaining and checking
sections.body:
A RAG system must be able to say it does not know. Two small, testable mechanisms:

1. **A relevance floor.** If even the best retrieved chunk scores below a threshold, answer `Not in the documents.` and do not generate. In our demo a keyword score of 4.5 separated the 22 answerable questions (lowest best score 4.94) from the 3 unanswerable ones (highest 3.88), so all 3 abstained correctly. That threshold was chosen after looking at these 25 questions, so it is optimistic. A threshold tuned on your test set will look better on that set than on new questions. Choose it on one set and check it on another.
2. **Checks on the generated text.** A cheap one: every number in the answer must appear in the cited chunk. Our `unsupported_numbers` function flags 'kept for 120 days' when the source says 90. It catches an invented figure; it does not catch a wrong claim made without numbers.

Beyond these, evaluation tools such as Ragas define LLM-judged metrics: **faithfulness** (is the answer supported by the retrieved context), **context precision** (are the retrieved chunks relevant), **context recall** (does the retrieved context cover what is needed, which needs a reference answer) and **response relevancy** (does the answer address the question). They use a model as the judge, so they inherit its errors; lesson 31 covers how far to trust them.

The code for the demo's answer step is short:

```python
"""Grounded answering around retrieval: access filter, abstention, citations and a crude faithfulness check.

The 'model' here is extractive (it quotes the best-matching sentence), so it cannot invent anything. That keeps
the pipeline testable without a key. `unsupported_numbers` is the kind of cheap guard you add around a real LLM.
"""
import re

from retrieve import Index, search, terms

ABSTAIN = "Not in the documents."


def best_sentence(question, body, idf):
    """Pick the sentence sharing the most (rarity-weighted) terms with the question. `body` excludes the title prefix."""
    q = set(terms(question))
    sentences = [s for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", body) if s]
    return max(sentences, key=lambda s: sum(idf.get(w, 0) for w in q & set(terms(s))))


def answer(index: Index, question, groups=(), threshold=4.5):
    """Return {'answer', 'citations'}. Chunks the caller may not see are filtered BEFORE ranking."""
    visible = lambda i: index.chunks[i]["acl"] in ("all", *groups)
    scores = index.bm25(question)
    top = search(index, question, "hybrid", top=3, allowed=visible)
    if not top or max(scores[i] for i in top) < threshold:
        return {"answer": ABSTAIN, "citations": []}
    best = index.chunks[top[0]]
    cites = [{"chunk": index.chunks[i]["id"], "title": index.chunks[i]["title"], "updated": index.chunks[i]["updated"]} for i in top[:1]]
    return {"answer": f"{best_sentence(question, best.get('body', best['text']), index.idf)} [{best['id']}]", "citations": cites}


def unsupported_numbers(answer_text, source_texts):
    """Numbers in the answer that appear in none of the sources: a cheap check for an invented figure."""
    source_numbers = set(re.findall(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)?", " ".join(source_texts)))
    return sorted(set(re.findall(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)?", re.sub(r"\[[^\]]*\]", "", answer_text))) - source_numbers)
```
sections.example: Fictional. 'Do we have a policy on working from another country?' The best chunk scores 1.75, below the 4.5 floor, so the system answers `Not in the documents.` instead of quoting an unrelated travel rule.
sections.common_mistake: Setting the abstention threshold on the same questions you then report results on, and quoting the result as if it were independent.
sections.check_question: Your system answers every question, including ones with no support in the documents. What are two things you add?
sections.check_answer: A relevance floor below which it abstains, and a test set that includes unanswerable questions so abstention is measured. Optionally a check that figures in the answer appear in the cited chunk.

sections.title: Do it: lab
sections.body:
1. Draw the pipeline from memory on one page: ingest, chunk, embed, store, retrieve, generate, cite. Then mark the six failure points F1 to F6 and write one sentence for each saying how you would notice it.
2. Run the reference pipeline (see lesson 30 for the code): `python demo.py` and `python evaluate.py` in the rag folder. Record the numbers.
3. From the output, find one question that failed at retrieval and one that retrieved the right document but gave the wrong answer. Label each with its failure point.
4. Run the access test: the same finance question for a caller with no groups and for a caller in the finance group. Save the output.
5. Add one unanswerable question of your own and one answerable question that uses different words from the document (a synonym). Does each behave as you predicted?

**Done when:** your diagram marks all six failure points, you have one real example each of a retrieval failure and an answer failure from the output, the access test shows two different answers, and your two new questions behave as you predicted (or you can say why not).

sections.title: Interview check
sections.body: Answer aloud first, then compare. Do not memorise the words; understand the shape.
sections.check_question: A stakeholder says 'the RAG chatbot hallucinated'. How do you investigate?
sections.check_answer:
1. Get the question, the answer, the chunks that were actually in the prompt, and their sources. Without the prompt contents I cannot tell failures apart.
2. Find the step: was the right document in the index (loading), was the fact intact in a chunk (chunking), was the right chunk retrieved and ranked high (retrieval, ranking), did the answer follow the chunk (generation), did the citation support the claim?
3. Fix at that step and add the question to a regression test set, with the right answer and the right source.
4. Report separately: retrieval hit rate and answer faithfulness, because they have different fixes and different owners.
5. Check security: was this user allowed to see every chunk in the prompt?

sections.title: Evidence to keep
sections.body: Keep the diagram, the numbers from your run, the two labelled failures and the access-test output. They are the evidence for lesson 30 and lesson 31.
